q: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent by definition?
o: GET
PUT
DELETE
POST
e:
Idempotent means: sending the same request once or ten times leaves the server in the same final state.
GET only reads. PUT sets a resource to a given value (setting it twice changes nothing more). DELETE removes it (deleting twice: still deleted).
POST usually CREATES something: two identical POSTs to `/orders` can create two orders. That is why retrying a POST is risky.
r: POST creates → repeating it can create duplicates.

q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
o: PUT creates a resource; PATCH deletes a resource
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH updates part of it
PATCH is idempotent by definition, but PUT is not
There is no difference, both update in the same way
e:
PUT sends the COMPLETE new version of a resource and replaces the old one. Fields you leave out may be reset.
PATCH sends only the fields that change, e.g. `{"email": "new@x.com"}`.
PUT is idempotent; PATCH is not guaranteed to be (e.g. 'add 1 to counter').
r: PUT = replace all. PATCH = change some fields.
fa: PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH applies a partial update

q: A logged-in user requests another tenant's invoice. Which status code is most appropriate?
o: 401 Unauthorized, because the user is not allowed
403 Forbidden (or 404, to hide that it exists)
400 Bad Request, because the id is not valid
500 Internal Server Error, because the access failed
e:
401 means 'I don't know who you are': credentials are missing or invalid (despite its name 'Unauthorized').
403 means 'I know who you are, but you are not allowed to do this'.
The user is logged in but the invoice is not theirs, so 403. Many APIs answer 404 instead, so attackers cannot even learn that the invoice exists.
r: 401 = who are you? 403 = you can't do that.
fa: 403 Forbidden (or 404 to hide existence)

q: A successful `POST /users` that creates a user should ideally return…
o: 200 OK with an empty body and no extra headers
201 Created with a `Location` header for the new resource
204 No Content with no body and no headers
302 Found with a redirect to the list of users
e:
201 Created tells the client precisely that something new was created.
The `Location` header gives the URL of the new resource (e.g. `/users/42`), and the body usually contains the created user.
200 means generic success; 204 means success with no body (common for DELETE).
r: Created something → 201 + Location.
fa: 201 Created with a `Location` header pointing to the new resource

q: FastAPI receives a body that fails Pydantic validation. Default response status?
e:
FastAPI validates the request body with Pydantic models. If a field is missing or has the wrong type, it automatically returns 422 Unprocessable Entity, with a list explaining which field failed and why.
Your endpoint code never runs. 400 is a more generic 'bad request'.
r: FastAPI validation error → 422.

q: A client exceeds the rate limit. Which status and header are standard?
o: 503 Service Unavailable with a `Cache-Control` header
429 Too Many Requests with a `Retry-After` header
403 Forbidden with a `WWW-Authenticate` header
400 Bad Request with a custom `X-Error` header
e:
429 Too Many Requests means 'you are sending requests too fast'.
The `Retry-After` header tells the client how many seconds to wait before trying again.
Good clients respect it and back off instead of hammering the server.
r: Rate limited → 429 + Retry-After.
fa: 429 Too Many Requests with `Retry-After`

q: Which statement about a standard signed JWT (JWS) is true?
o: Its payload is encrypted, so nobody except the server can read it
Its payload is only base64url-encoded; the signature stops edits
It can be revoked at once on the server side by default
It must always be stored in the localStorage of the browser
e:
A JWT has three parts: header.payload.signature. The payload is only encoded (base64url), NOT encrypted: anyone can decode and read it (try jwt.io).
The signature, made with the server's secret key, proves the token was issued by the server and not modified. If someone changes the payload, the signature no longer matches.
So never put passwords or secrets in a JWT.
r: JWT payload is readable by anyone; the signature only stops tampering.
fa: Its payload is only base64url-encoded; anyone can read it, but the signature prevents tampering

q: Main drawback of stateless JWT access tokens?
o: They are too large to send
They are hard to revoke before expiry
They require a database lookup on every request
They only work with OAuth
e:
The server validates a JWT just by checking its signature and expiry, without looking anything up. That is fast, but it also means the server cannot easily 'cancel' a token: it stays valid until it expires.
Common solutions: short-lived access tokens (5-15 minutes) plus refresh tokens that CAN be revoked, or a denylist of revoked token IDs.
r: JWTs are hard to revoke → keep them short-lived.

q: For a browser web app, where is a session/auth token safest from XSS theft?
o: In localStorage, where scripts of the page can read it
In a global JavaScript variable inside the page
In an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie
In the URL query string of each request
e:
If an attacker injects JavaScript into your page (XSS), that script can read localStorage and JS variables and send your token away.
An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript at all; the browser just sends it with requests. Secure = only over HTTPS; SameSite = not sent on most cross-site requests.
Cookies need CSRF protection, which SameSite mostly provides.
r: Auth token in a browser → HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie.
fa: An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie

q: Which OAuth 2.0 flow is recommended for single-page apps and mobile apps?
o: Implicit flow
Resource Owner Password Credentials
Authorization Code with PKCE
Client Credentials
e:
Apps running on a user's device cannot keep a secret (anyone can inspect the code).
Authorization Code + PKCE adds a one-time random 'proof' so that even if someone steals the authorization code, they cannot exchange it for tokens.
The Implicit and Password flows are deprecated. Client Credentials is for server-to-server calls with no user.
r: Browser/mobile login with OAuth → Authorization Code + PKCE.

q: What is middleware in a web framework?
o: A database driver that connects the app to the database engine
Code that wraps each request and response, like logging or auth
A frontend library that is used for building user interfaces
A message broker that delivers events between the services
e:
Middleware is code that runs before and/or after EVERY request, around your endpoint functions, like layers of an onion.
Typical uses: logging, measuring response time, checking authentication, adding CORS headers, handling errors.
The order matters: e.g. authentication must run before your route logic.
r: Middleware = code that runs around every request.
fa: Code that wraps every request/response, e.g. logging, auth, CORS, timing

q: Which statement about CORS is correct?
o: It protects your API from curl and from server-to-server calls
It is enforced by browsers; the server lists the allowed origins
It encrypts the traffic that moves between browser and server
It replaces authentication on the API for trusted websites
e:
Browsers block a web page from reading responses from a different origin (domain/port) by default: the same-origin policy.
CORS is how a server says 'it's OK, pages from https://myapp.com may read my responses', via `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
Only browsers enforce it. curl, Postman or another server ignore CORS completely, so it is not a security wall for your API.
r: CORS is a browser rule, not API protection.
fa: It is enforced by browsers; the server declares allowed origins via `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`

q: Listing 50 orders then accessing `order.customer.name` in a loop triggers 51 queries. In Django, the usual fix for this foreign key is…
o: `prefetch_related("customer")`
`select_related("customer")`
`.only("customer")`
e:
This is the N+1 problem: 1 query to get the orders, then 1 extra query per order to fetch its customer.
`select_related("customer")` loads orders and customers together in one query with a SQL JOIN.
`prefetch_related` uses a second query for all related rows at once (for many-to-many or reverse relations). In SQLAlchemy: `joinedload` / `selectinload`.
r: Loop that queries per item = N+1. Load related data up front.

q: In SQLAlchemy, what is the `Session` primarily?
o: An HTTP session that identifies the user who is logged in
A unit of work that tracks loaded objects and flushes changes
A connection string that points to the database server
A migration tool that changes the schema of the database
e:
The SQLAlchemy Session keeps track of the objects you loaded or added. When you change them, it remembers what changed.
On `commit()`, it sends all the changes to the database together as one transaction.
Use one session per request (or unit of work), and never share a session between threads.
r: Session = tracks your changes and commits them together.
fa: A unit of work that tracks loaded objects and flushes changes in a transaction

q: What does `Depends(get_db)` in a FastAPI endpoint signature do?
o: It declares a Python import that the function needs in order to run
It calls `get_db` and injects the result, with cleanup after yield
It creates a background task that runs after the response
It validates the response of the endpoint before it is sent
e:
FastAPI sees `db = Depends(get_db)`, calls `get_db()` for each request and passes the result into your function.
If `get_db` uses `yield`, the code after yield (e.g. closing the DB session) runs after the response.
In tests you can replace it: `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_db`.
r: Depends = FastAPI's dependency injection.
fa: Tells FastAPI to call `get_db` and inject its result (dependency injection), including generator cleanup

q: In FastAPI you must call a slow, blocking SDK. Which option avoids blocking the event loop?
o: Call it directly inside an `async def` endpoint, as usual
Use a plain `def` endpoint, or wrap it with `asyncio.to_thread`
Add `await` in front of the synchronous call to the SDK
Increase the timeout of the server so that the call can finish
e:
`async def` endpoints run directly on the event loop, which must never be blocked.
FastAPI runs plain `def` endpoints in a pool of worker threads, so a blocking call only blocks that thread.
Inside async code, `await asyncio.to_thread(sdk.call)` moves the blocking call to a thread. You cannot `await` a normal (non-async) function.
r: Blocking library → plain def endpoint or to_thread.
fa: Declare the endpoint with plain `def` (runs in a threadpool) or wrap the call with `run_in_threadpool`/`asyncio.to_thread`

q: WSGI vs ASGI: what does ASGI add?
o: Template rendering for HTML pages on the server side
Async support, including WebSockets and long-lived connections
An ORM that maps database tables to Python classes
Static file serving, and nothing else on top of WSGI
e:
WSGI and ASGI are standards for how a Python web server talks to your web app.
WSGI (Flask, classic Django, served by Gunicorn) is synchronous: one request per worker at a time, plain request/response.
ASGI (FastAPI, modern Django, served by Uvicorn) supports async code, WebSockets and long-lived connections.
r: WSGI = sync. ASGI = async + WebSockets.
fa: Async support including WebSockets and long-lived connections

q: Why is cursor (keyset) pagination preferred over `OFFSET` for large, changing datasets?
o: It supports jumping directly to any page number of the results
OFFSET skips rows and slows down; a cursor uses an index
Cursor pagination does not need any index on the table
OFFSET is not valid SQL in most of the databases
e:
`OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20` makes the database read and throw away 100,000 rows, so deep pages are slow. If rows are inserted while the user pages, items can be skipped or shown twice.
Cursor pagination remembers the last item seen and asks for `WHERE id > 12345 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`, which uses an index and is always fast and stable.
Trade-off: no 'jump to page 37'.
r: Large or live lists → cursor pagination.
fa: OFFSET gets slower as it grows and can skip/duplicate rows when data changes; a cursor seeks with an indexed `WHERE id > :last`

q: Which REST constraint means each request carries all information needed to process it?
o: Uniform interface
Statelessness
Cacheability
Layered system
e:
Stateless: the server does not remember anything about the client between requests. Each request brings everything needed, e.g. an auth token.
Benefit: any server instance can handle any request, so you can add servers behind a load balancer easily.
User data still lives in the database; 'stateless' refers to the server process memory.
r: Stateless = every request is self-contained.

q: A mobile app retries a payment POST after a timeout. How do you prevent a double charge?
o: Use GET instead of POST for the payment requests of the app
Send an `Idempotency-Key` header; the server returns the first result
Disable all the retries in the mobile app after a timeout
Return a 500 error to the client on the second call
e:
The timeout might have happened AFTER the server charged the card, so the client cannot know if the first try worked.
The client generates a unique key (a UUID) per payment attempt and sends it with every retry.
The server saves the key with the result. If the same key arrives again, it returns the saved result instead of charging again. Stripe's API works this way.
r: Retries of POST → Idempotency-Key.
fa: Have the client send an `Idempotency-Key` header; the server stores the key and returns the original result on repeats

q: Which rate limiting algorithm naturally allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate?
o: Fixed window counter
Token bucket
Round robin
FIFO queue
e:
Picture a bucket that receives tokens at a fixed rate (e.g. 10 per second) up to a maximum (e.g. 50). Each request takes one token; no token, request rejected.
If a client was quiet, the bucket fills up, so it can send a short burst of 50 at once; over time it can never exceed 10 per second.
Fixed windows are simpler but allow double bursts at window edges.
r: Token bucket = steady average + allowed bursts.

q: What does gRPC typically offer over JSON/REST?
o: Human-readable payloads that are easy to inspect by hand
Binary Protobuf over HTTP/2, strict contracts and streaming
Native browser support, without any proxy in between
No need for schemas, because messages describe themselves
e:
gRPC defines services and messages in a `.proto` file and generates client and server code from it, so both sides share a strict contract.
Messages are compact binary (Protobuf) over HTTP/2, which is fast and supports streaming in both directions.
Great for internal service-to-service calls. Downsides: not readable by humans, and browsers need a proxy (gRPC-Web).
r: gRPC = fast, typed, binary; best between internal services.
fa: Binary Protobuf messages over HTTP/2, strict contracts and bidirectional streaming

q: In GraphQL, resolving `posts { author { name } }` naively causes many DB queries. Common fix?
o: Use REST endpoints instead of GraphQL for the nested data
Batch and cache the lookups per request with a DataLoader
Add more indexes to the tables of the database that is used
Disable the nested fields in the schema for all the clients
e:
GraphQL calls a resolver function per field. For 50 posts, the `author` resolver runs 50 times = 50 queries (the N+1 problem again).
A DataLoader collects all author IDs requested in the same moment and loads them in ONE query (`WHERE id IN (...)`), then hands each resolver its author.
r: GraphQL N+1 → DataLoader batching.
fa: Batch and cache per request with a DataLoader

q: How should your service verify incoming webhooks from a provider?
o: Check the User-Agent header that comes with the request
Verify an HMAC signature of the raw body, plus a timestamp
Only accept requests that arrive over a secure HTTPS connection
Trust any request that is sent to a secret, hard-to-guess URL
e:
A webhook is the provider calling YOUR URL. Anyone on the internet could call that URL with fake data.
The provider signs each payload with a shared secret (HMAC). You recompute the signature over the raw body and compare (with `hmac.compare_digest`). If it matches, the data is genuine.
Also reject old timestamps (replayed messages) and handle duplicates, because providers retry.
r: Webhooks: verify the HMAC signature, reject old timestamps.
fa: Verify an HMAC signature over the raw body with the shared secret, plus a timestamp to prevent replays

q: An endpoint generates a 2-minute report. Best API design?
o: Keep the HTTP request open for the full two minutes
Enqueue a job, return 202 Accepted with a status URL, then poll
Return a 500 error and ask the client to retry later
Use a GET request with a very large timeout on the client
e:
Load balancers and proxies usually cut connections after 30-60 seconds, and a user staring at a spinner is bad UX.
Instead: put the job in a queue, answer immediately with 202 Accepted and a URL like `/reports/123/status`. A background worker does the work.
The client checks the status URL (polling) or gets notified (webhook/WebSocket) when it is ready.
r: Slow work → background job + 202 Accepted.
fa: Enqueue a job (Celery/RQ/SQS), return 202 Accepted with a status URL, let the client poll or receive a webhook

q: A client sends `If-None-Match: "abc123"` and the resource is unchanged. Server response?
o: 200 OK with the full body of the resource
304 Not Modified with no body
204 No Content with no body
412 Precondition Failed with an error
e:
An ETag is a version fingerprint the server sends with a response. The client stores it.
Next time, the client sends `If-None-Match: <etag>`. If nothing changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified with an empty body, and the client reuses its cached copy. This saves bandwidth.
For updates, `If-Match` prevents overwriting someone else's change (412 if the version is old).
r: Same ETag → 304, reuse the cache.

q: A common starting point for the number of Gunicorn sync workers is…
o: 1 per server
(2 × CPU cores) + 1
100 per core
Equal to RAM in GB
e:
Each sync worker handles one request at a time. More workers = more requests in parallel, but each uses memory and CPU.
The Gunicorn docs suggest (2 × cores) + 1 as a starting point (for 4 cores: 9 workers), then tune it with load tests.
For I/O-heavy apps, async workers (Uvicorn) or threads can handle many more connections.
r: Start with 2 × cores + 1, then measure.

q: Which API versioning approach is most common and explicit in public REST APIs?
o: Version in the URL path (`/v1/orders`)
Changing the field names silently
Using a different port per version
Never versioning the API at all
e:
Clients integrate against your API and break if you change it. Versioning lets you release breaking changes as a new version while old clients keep working.
Putting it in the path (`/v1/`, `/v2/`) is the most visible and common. Alternatives: a header or a query parameter.
Announce deprecations early and keep old versions running for a while.
r: Breaking API change → new version (/v2).

q: Design a REST API for a bookings resource (hotel rooms). What endpoints, codes and concerns?
a:
- Resources: `GET /rooms?from=&to=` (availability), `POST /bookings` (201 + Location), `GET /bookings/{id}`, `PATCH /bookings/{id}` (change dates), `POST /bookings/{id}/cancel` or `DELETE` (200/204).
- Errors: 400/422 validation, 401/403 auth, 404 missing, 409 conflict (room already booked), 429 rate limit.
- Concurrency: prevent double booking with a DB constraint or a transaction with row lock / version check.
- Idempotency-Key on POST; cursor pagination on lists; filter and sort parameters.
- Auth (OAuth/JWT), ownership checks, consistent error format, versioning `/v1`, OpenAPI docs.

q: How would you secure a REST API end to end?
a:
- TLS everywhere; HSTS.
- Authentication: OAuth 2.0/OIDC or short-lived JWT + refresh; validate signature, `exp`, `aud`, `iss`, allowed algorithms.
- Authorization on every request at object level (prevent IDOR); least privilege, scopes/roles.
- Validate input with schemas (Pydantic); parameterized queries; limit payload sizes.
- Rate limiting and abuse detection; MFA and lockout for login.
- Secrets in a secret manager; rotate keys.
- Safe error messages (no stack traces), security headers, strict CORS.
- Audit logs, dependency scanning, monitoring and alerts.

q: What is an API?
o: A programming language that is used to build servers
A defined way for one program to request data or actions from another
A type of database that stores the request logs of an app
A visual design tool that is used to draw interfaces
e:
API means Application Programming Interface: the 'menu' a system offers to other programs. It lists what you can ask for and in what format, and hides how it works inside.
A web API is reached over HTTP. Example: a weather app sends `GET https://api.weather.com/today?city=Lima` and receives JSON with the forecast.
r: API = a contract for programs to talk to each other.
fa: A defined way for one program to request data or actions from another, e.g. over HTTP

q: Which list contains the main parts of an HTTP request?
o: Method, URL, headers, optional body
Port, cookie, password, session id
HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images
Status code, reason phrase and body only
e:
An HTTP request has:
- Method: what to do (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
- URL: which resource (`/users/42`).
- Headers: extra information (`Authorization`, `Content-Type`).
- Body (optional): data you send, usually JSON, for POST/PUT/PATCH.
The RESPONSE has a status code, headers and a body.
r: Request = method + URL + headers + body.

q: What is the purpose of a GET request?
o: Create a new resource on the server side
Retrieve data without changing anything
Delete data that is stored on the server
Upload files from the client to the server
e:
GET asks the server for data. It must be 'safe': it should not create, change or delete anything.
Because of that, browsers, proxies and CDNs may cache and repeat GET requests freely.
Never use GET for actions like `/delete-user?id=5`: a crawler or prefetch could trigger it.
r: GET = read only.
fa: Retrieve data without changing anything on the server

q: What do HTTP status codes starting with 2, 4 and 5 mean?
o: 2xx is an error, 4xx is success, 5xx is a redirect
2xx is success, 4xx is a client error, 5xx is a server error
All three groups mean that the request was a success
2xx is a redirect, 4xx is success, 5xx is a client error
e:
The first digit tells the category:
- 2xx: success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content).
- 3xx: redirect (301, 302, 304).
- 4xx: the client did something wrong (400 bad data, 401 not logged in, 403 forbidden, 404 not found).
- 5xx: the server failed (500 bug, 502/503 server down or overloaded).
r: 2 = OK, 4 = your fault, 5 = server's fault.
fa: 2xx success, 4xx client error (your request is wrong), 5xx server error (the server failed)

q: `GET /users/9999` and that user does not exist. Correct status code?
o: 200 with empty body
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
401 Unauthorized
e:
404 Not Found means the requested resource does not exist.
Returning 200 with an empty body confuses clients, who think it worked. 500 would suggest the server crashed, which is not the case.
r: Resource doesn't exist → 404.

q: Your API returns 500 Internal Server Error. What does that usually indicate?
o: The user typed a wrong password when they tried to log in
An unexpected error in the server code, like an unhandled exception
The resource was not found at the URL that was requested
The request succeeded and the server returned the data
e:
500 means the server failed in a way it did not expect: often an exception nobody caught (a bug), or a crashed dependency.
The client cannot fix it by changing the request. Check the server logs and the stack trace.
Good APIs catch known problems and return a specific 4xx code instead.
r: 500 = bug or crash on the server. Check the logs.
fa: An unexpected error in the server code, e.g. an unhandled exception

q: What is JSON?
o: A JavaScript framework that is used for building web apps
A lightweight text format for data, with `{}` objects and `[]` arrays
A database engine that stores documents as binary files
A binary image format that is commonly used on the web
e:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is plain text that both humans and programs read easily: `{"name": "Ana", "skills": ["python", "sql"]}`.
It is the most common format for API requests and responses.
In Python, `json.dumps(obj)` turns a dict into JSON text and `json.loads(text)` does the reverse.
r: JSON = the text format APIs speak.
fa: A lightweight text format for data, with objects `{}` and arrays `[]`

q: In `GET /users/42/orders?status=paid&limit=10`, which are the path parameter and the query parameters?
o: Path: status. Query: 42 and limit
Path: 42 (the user). Query: status and limit
Both are query parameters of the request
The URL does not contain any parameters
e:
Path parameters are part of the URL path and usually identify a specific resource: `/users/42` → user 42.
Query parameters come after `?`, separated by `&`, and usually filter, sort or paginate: `status=paid`, `limit=10`.
In FastAPI: `def orders(user_id: int, status: str | None = None, limit: int = 10)`.
r: Path = which resource. Query = how to filter it.
fa: Path: 42 (identifies the user); query: status and limit (filter/options)

q: Which endpoint follows REST naming conventions?
o: `POST /createUser`
`GET /getUserById?id=42`
`GET /users/42`
`GET /user_delete/42`
e:
REST URLs name RESOURCES (nouns, usually plural), and the HTTP method says the action:
- `GET /users/42` read user 42
- `POST /users` create a user
- `PATCH /users/42` update
- `DELETE /users/42` delete
Putting verbs in the URL (`/createUser`) repeats what the method already says.
r: Nouns in the URL, verbs in the HTTP method.

q: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
o: Only faster page loads, mostly on slow mobile networks
Encryption and server identity checks via TLS, so data is safe
A different data format for the requests and the responses
Automatic login for the visitors that return to the site
e:
With plain HTTP, anyone on the same Wi-Fi or network path can read and modify the traffic, including passwords.
HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS: the data is encrypted, protected against tampering, and the certificate proves you are talking to the real server.
Today every site and API should use HTTPS.
r: HTTPS = HTTP + encryption + identity check.
fa: Encryption and server identity verification via TLS, so data cannot be read or changed in transit

q: What does the request header `Content-Type: application/json` tell the server?
o: The client wants JSON back in the response
The body of this request is formatted as JSON
The request is encrypted before it is sent
The user is already logged in
e:
`Content-Type` describes the format of the body being SENT. With `application/json` the server knows to parse the body as JSON.
To say which format you want BACK, the client uses the `Accept` header.
If the header is wrong or missing, many frameworks reject or misread the body.
r: Content-Type = format of what I send. Accept = format I want back.

q: In FastAPI, what does `@app.get("/items/{item_id}")` above a function do?
o: It downloads an item from the server to the client
It registers a GET route; `item_id` is taken from the URL
It creates a database table named items for the function
It defines a test case for the function underneath it
e:
Routing connects a URL + HTTP method to a Python function (an endpoint).
When a request `GET /items/7` arrives, FastAPI calls your function with `item_id=7`, converting it to the type you declared (e.g. int).
Whatever the function returns (dict, Pydantic model) is turned into the JSON response.
r: Route = method + path → function.
fa: Registers a route: GET requests to /items/<id> are handled by that function, with item_id taken from the URL

q: What is the backend of a web application?
o: The server part: business logic, data access and security
The visual design of the pages that the users see
The browser in which the user opens the application
Only the database in which the data is stored
e:
The backend is the code and systems running on servers.
It receives requests from the frontend, applies the rules of the business (for example 'a user cannot buy more items than the stock'), reads or writes the database, checks who is logged in, and sends back a response.
Typical backend technologies: Java with Spring Boot, Python with FastAPI or Django, Node.js.
r: Backend = server-side logic, data and security.
fa: The part on servers that holds the business logic, talks to the database and checks security; users never see it directly

q: What is a server?
o: A very expensive computer that only large companies can own
A computer or program that waits for requests and sends responses
A type of database that is used to store the user data
A programming language that is used mainly for backends
e:
The word has two meanings and both are used.
Hardware: a computer connected to a network that stores files and runs programs for others.
Software: a program that listens for requests (for example a web server that understands HTTP) and answers them.
A server can be your laptop while you develop, or a machine in a cloud data center in production.
r: Server = waits for requests and answers them.
fa: A computer or program that waits for requests from clients and sends back responses

q: In 'client and server', what is a client?
o: The person who pays for the software that is being built
Whoever starts a request: a browser, an app or another program
The database in which the data of the system is stored
The operating system that runs on the server machine
e:
The client asks, the server answers.
Your browser is a client when it requests a web page. A mobile app is a client when it asks the backend for your orders. A backend can also be a client of another service.
In HTTP, the client always starts the conversation and the server answers.
r: Client = the one who sends the request.
fa: Whoever starts a request: a browser, a phone app, or even another program

q: What does 'full-stack developer' mean?
o: Someone who works only on databases and on their queries
Someone who works on both the frontend and the backend
Someone who has a full-time contract with a company
Someone who knows every programming language that exists
e:
The 'stack' is the set of technology layers an application is made of: frontend, backend, database, and infrastructure.
A full-stack developer is comfortable across those layers. It does not mean an expert in all of them, but able to build a feature end to end.
Example stack: React (frontend) + Spring Boot (backend) + PostgreSQL (database).
r: Full-stack = frontend + backend.
fa: Someone who can work on both the frontend and the backend (and usually the database and deployment basics)

q: Restaurant analogy: the customer orders from a waiter, who takes the order to the kitchen and brings back the food. Which part is the API?
o: The customer, who makes the order and waits for the food
The waiter: the agreed way to ask the kitchen and get an answer
The kitchen, where the food is made and then served
The price list, which the customer reads before ordering
e:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract about how programs talk to each other.
- Customer = the client app (browser, mobile app).
- Waiter = the API: you order using the menu (the documented requests), and you get a response.
- Kitchen = the backend that does the real work.
The customer does not need to know how the kitchen works, only how to order.
r: API = the waiter between client and backend.
fa: The waiter: the agreed way to ask the kitchen for something and get an answer, without entering the kitchen

q: What is HTTP?
o: A programming language that is used for building web pages
The protocol browsers and servers use: a request, then a response
A type of database that is used for storing web data
An antivirus program that scans the traffic of the web
e:
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the language of the web. A request has a method (like GET), a path and optional headers and body. A response has a status code (like 200 or 404), headers and usually a body.
It is a client-server protocol: the client always starts the conversation.
HTTPS is HTTP inside an encrypted connection.
r: HTTP = how clients and servers talk on the web.
fa: The set of rules (protocol) that browsers and servers use to exchange web pages and data: a client sends a request and the server sends a response

q: In the address `https://api.shop.com/products?id=7`, which part is the path?
o: https
api.shop.com
/products
id=7
e:
A URL is made of parts:
- `https` is the scheme (protocol).
- `api.shop.com` is the host (the server's domain name).
- `/products` is the path (which resource on that server).
- `?id=7` is the query string (extra parameters).
The port is hidden: HTTPS uses 443 by default and HTTP uses 80.
r: URL = scheme + host + path + query.

q: Which sentence best describes REST?
o: A database engine that is designed for storing web data
A style for web APIs: resources with URLs, acted on by HTTP methods
A security protocol that is used for logins and sessions
A JavaScript framework that is used for building frontends
e:
REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style described by Roy Fielding in his doctoral dissertation (2000). It is not a library or a protocol.
In practice: `GET /users/42` reads user 42, `POST /users` creates one, `DELETE /users/42` removes it.
Its constraints include client-server, stateless requests, cacheable responses and a uniform interface.
r: REST = resources + URLs + HTTP methods.
fa: A style for designing web APIs: things are resources with URLs, and the standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) act on them

q: What does a backend web framework such as Spring Boot, FastAPI or Django do for you?
o: It gives ready-made blocks: routing, JSON and database access
It replaces the need for a database in the application
It designs the screens and the pages that users will see
It makes the physical server faster by tuning the hardware
e:
Without a framework you would write by hand how to read network requests, parse data and match URLs.
A framework solves those repeated problems so you write only your own logic.
Example: in Spring Boot you write a method and mark it with `@GetMapping("/hello")`, and the framework calls it when someone visits `/hello`.
r: Framework = reusable foundation for server code.
fa: It provides ready-made building blocks for common server tasks: receiving requests, routing URLs to your code, reading JSON, talking to databases

q: In an HTTP conversation, who sends the first message?
o: The server, with a welcome message
The client, with a request
Both of them at the same time
The database, with a query
e:
HTTP always works as request then response.
The client (usually a browser or app) sends the request, and the server answers. A server does not normally start sending to a client by itself.
For live updates (chat, notifications) there are other mechanisms such as WebSockets.
r: Client asks first, server answers.
